pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: In your own words: what does Big-O notation measure, and why do we throw away constant factors and lower-order terms like the 5n in n^2 + 5n?
expected_points: it measures how the number of basic operations grows as input size grows, not seconds
worst case by default
constants depend on hardware/implementation and don't change the growth shape
for large n the dominant term dwarfs the rest, so lower-order terms are noise

questions.prompt: Rank these from best to worst — O(n log n), O(1), O(2^n), O(n), O(log n), O(n^2) — and give one concrete example algorithm or code shape for each.
expected_points: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n)

examples such as: array index / first element (O(1)), repeated halving like dictionary lookup (O(log n)), summing a list (O(n)), good sorting (O(n log n)), comparing every pair (O(n^2)), trying every subset (O(2^n))

questions.prompt: A function loops over the input once, then has a second loop nested inside a third that both run over the whole input. What's the total complexity, and what are the rules you applied?
expected_points: sequential loops add: n + n^2
nested loops that both scale with n multiply: n * n = n^2
addition keeps only the dominant term, so the total is O(n^2)
bonus: an inner loop with a constant bound would NOT multiply — it stays O(n)

questions.prompt: Your HasDuplicate and HasDuplicateSorted solve the same problem. What is the auxiliary space of each, and why doesn't the input slice count toward it?
expected_points: HasDuplicate allocates a map with up to one entry per element: O(n) auxiliary space
HasDuplicateSorted uses a couple of variables: O(1) auxiliary space
auxiliary space counts only memory the algorithm allocates on top of its input; the caller already paid for the slice

questions.prompt: You need duplicate detection on an unsorted slice inside a memory-starved embedded device, and separately inside a beefy web server. Which approach do you pick in each place, and how do you justify it?
expected_points: embedded: the O(n^2)-time / O(1)-space pair comparison — no allocation, and n is often small
server: the O(n)-time / O(n)-space map — memory is cheap there and n can be large
the justification names both costs explicitly rather than calling one option 'better' absolutely

questions.prompt: A colleague benchmarks your O(n) function against their O(n^2) one on 20-element inputs and theirs wins. Is Big-O broken?
expected_points: no — Big-O describes growth for large n, not absolute speed at a fixed small n
constants and setup costs (like allocating a map) can dominate at small sizes
grow the input and the O(n) version must eventually win

questions.prompt: In Go, what's the time complexity of building a big string by doing s = s + piece inside a loop that runs n times, and why?
expected_points: strings are immutable, so each + copies the whole string built so far
copy work is 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is O(n^2)
a single loop can still be quadratic when each iteration does O(n) hidden work; strings.Builder keeps it linear
